title: Wind-up elastic robot jumps forever when fed infrared light
description:
Robots – that is, self-guided mechanisms interacting with or changing their environments – exist in the popular imagination as large, blocky, metallic beings like R2D2 or TARS from Interstellar. But the field of soft robotics offers a vast array of robotic limbs, sensors, and body types that greatly expand our understanding of what shapes a robot can manifest and what tasks it can perform.

title: Survey Mark Data
description:
Sources of survey data

This list contains both professional data and information for recreational hunters, so please note the source of each and evaluate accordingly. Also note that some sources, USGS datasheets in particular, contain many superseded marks that are no longer reliable for survey purposes but are very useful for recreational survey mark hunting.

Professional resources

NGS Database: Datasheets and Survey Mark Recovery
Search/browse the main authoritative source of official survey data for the United States.
USGS Datasheets
USGS datasheets I have obtained and scanned. USGS does not offer digitized datasheets.
OPUS Shared Solutions Dashboard
Local Control Monument Databases
Survey data from U.S. states, counties, and cities, as well as a few international resources
NOAA Tides & Currents Bench Mark Data Sheets
Tidal benchmark station locations and descriptions
The NOAA CORS Network (NCN) Web Map
U-SMART
USACE (Army Corps of Engineers) Survey Monument Archival & Retrieval Tool
Yellowstone National Park Benchmark Database
Data and photos of over 500 benchmarks in Yellowstone National Park, many of which are still used for gravity and GPS observations

Recreational resources

Bench Mark Database
UK-based recreational benchmark hunting site
The Corner Corner
Search for locations where multiple states meet at a point.
Disney Benchmarks Pages by Patty Winter
Disney World Surveying Benchmarks
Waymarking search for “survey markers”
A resource for recreational survey mark hunters

Selected historical data

These sources represent the types of historical documents I often consult when searching for marks, and are specific to the areas I search. You will likely find similar resources for other areas by searching Google Books, the NOAA Library, the NGS Publications Library, and the USGS Publications Warehouse.

Bulletin 46: Work of the New Jersey Geodetic Control Survey, c. 1938
Precise Leveling in New York City
By Frederick W. Koop. Executed 1909 to 1914.
Results of Spirit Leveling in Arizona. 1899 to 1915, inclusive.
Spirit Leveling in Maine, 1899-1915
By R. B. Marshall. 1916.
Triangulation and Primary Traverse, 1913-1915
This USGS Bulletin (#644) provides data and descriptions for triangulation and traverse stations determined between 1913 and 1915. The full document is a large file (205MB); USGS has this file broken down by state/region at USGS Publication Warehouse.
Triangulation in Arizona
“1927 datum. Part 1: First- and second-order triangulation in south central part of state, by Clement L. Garner. 1941.”
Triangulation in Maine
By Walter F. Reynolds. 1918.

For airway beacons in the eastern U.S., see: Airway Beacons List—Eastern U.S.

title: MoMA explores the useful beauty of information design
description:
When people post infographics on their Instagram accounts, they’re sharing information and facts about the world with their followers. They’re also trying to convey something about the kind of person they are by distributing these aesthetically pleasing, digestible bites of data. Perhaps they want to make a statement about their own politics or conscientiousness. 

So what is the Museum of Modern Art revealing about itself as an institution with its forthcoming exhibit Full Disclosure: The Edge of Information Design?

The pieces of information design in the exhibition “tell us the fact that the museum is always ready to understand what’s important to the world in that particular moment, and to try to give the best examples of it,” says Paola Antonelli, the senior curator of architecture and design at New York City’s MoMA, during a walkthrough of the exhibit as she and her team prepared it for its opening on September 27. “Having an exhibition about information design shows that we’re continuing our mission to talk about the art in our time, of our time.”

The first piece that visitors will see upon entrance through the museum is Warming Stripes, by climatologist Ed Hawkins, who “wanted to find a way to drill it in people’s brains that global warming is really happening.” The stripes, which over the course of the work go from a deep blue to a bright red, represent the average temperature of each year. The imagery resembles a gorgeous rug—and also a huge warning sign. 

To Antonelli, Warming Stripes is an ideal distillation of information design, because the field “takes phenomena big and small, public and intimate, complex, scientific, and statistically more superficial, and renders them in a way that is comprehensible by a wide audience.”

The exhibition shows that information design is not limited to weaving huge data sets into legibility. One portion of Full Disclosure focuses entirely on personal data, and includes a correspondence between artists Giorgia Lupi and Stefanie Posavec. In what became their Dear Data project, the two found creative ways to visualize how many times they cursed in a week, for example. The idea is that the practice of information design can help people connect in a more personal or even playful way with the many nuggets of data that have come to symbolize their lives. 

MoMA has been collecting works of information design since 2008, when Antonelli debuted an exhibition called Design and the Elastic Mind, which focused on the ways designers have adapted to revolutionary scientific change. As part of her curation, she encountered “all of these different designers that didn’t really have a home,” who worked with data visualization, she says. “I kind of hugged them up.” All but one of the pieces in this exhibition are part of MoMA’s collection.

Often, the origination of information design as a practice gets traced back to the invention of the bar chart or Dr. John Snow’s 19th-century map of cholera in London. But Antonelli sees it going back way further—it has always been a part of the human experience because “it’s all about explaining things in a narrative and visual way.” That means cave drawings displaying the haul of deer from a hunt fit the bill, too. 

But the use of computers and digital tools has exploded and expanded the practice of information design. And the exhibition reflects that. 

While many people encounter examples of information design on tiny phone screens, and there are ample opportunities to interact with screens in this exhibition, it also includes massive pieces that take up entire walls or, in the case of Kate Crawford and Vladan Joler’s Calculating Empires, one room. 

Newspapers and media companies often have teams focused on information design, and two works from The New York Times are included in the exhibition—one that uses 3-D rendering to explain why Paris’s Notre Dame cathedral was so vulnerable to fire and another that recreates the Greenwood neighborhood destroyed by the Tulsa race massacre. 

Antonelli sees the museum’s first-ever exhibition focused entirely on information design as a “gentle provocation,” or perhaps a “surprise” reminder that everyday works—say, those found in a newspaper—are museum-worthy.

She wants visitors to leave with a better sense of discernment for the barrage of infographics and diagrams they’ll encounter each day. She hopes they’ll use their own critical sensibility to see how the creator’s choice of color, typeface, or other formal decisions might impact how a viewer sees what it’s trying to represent. And she’d like people who see these design examples to have a keener sense of appreciation for when something has been done “elegantly and efficiently.”

“We’re hoping that, as usual, they will look at their life with different eyes,” Antonelli says. “More critical eyes.”

title: Replacing the old battery on rechargeable bike lights
description:
Hello! Recently I needed bike lights for my bike. And I remembered that I already had rechargeable bike lights that I bought ten years ago, that I hadn’t tried in a long time. I tried to recharge them, but after fully charging them, they only worked for maybe 5 minutes before they turned off again.

I don’t know much about electronics, but I’ve been curious about whether it’s possible to fix old electronics for a long time, and this seemed like the perfect repair project because I might just need to replace the battery.

So I went to the local queer makerspace where I’m a member to use the soldering iron and try to do it! I don’t know much about electronics and this post does not contain any safety advice because I don’t know much about safety. I think it’s nice to do projects in a community space where you can get help.

step 1: cut it open

The bike light felt like it was made of silicone, so I cut open the silicone in a haphazard way along something that vaguely looked like a seam.

I definitely ripped some silicone in the process and it was pretty messy but I got it open and found the circuit board.

I don’t know the model number of the bike lights but there’s a photo of them at the end of the post.

step 2: remove the screws

There were some screws attaching things together so I removed them so I could get the circuit board out.

Mostly I tried to remove as few screws as possible because I was worried about losing them or not being able to put them back after. I probably put the screws in a bag or something.

step 3: get the circuit board out

I took out the circuit board. Here’s what it looked like:

You can see where the battery is attached, I think it’s left of RI3 and above Q2.

Here’s what the battery looked like:

step 4: desolder the battery

I’d never desoldered anything before, so I found the iFixit guide to desoldering and read it. Also I asked my friends Lee and Lauria for advice.

Here were the steps I ended up following based on the guide & the advice I got:

  1. Use a desoldering pump to remove most of the solder
  2. Once most of it is gone, kind of pull them apart to try to separate them
  3. Also try to avoid getting the battery too hot in the process by taking breaks to let it cool down. I’m not very good with a soldering iron so it took a while.
  4. The battery has an attachment that is welded to the top. For a while I thought I needed to remove this and it seemed impossible, but it turned out the replacement battery comes with that part so actually I was supposed to leave it alone.

step 5: identify the battery

In the picture of the battery in Step 3, you can see it says something like “3” and “LI???77”. There’s a piece of metal that I think is welded or something to the top of the battery. It seemed impossible and also maybe not smart to try to remove so I wasn’t sure how to find out what an “LI????77” was or how to order another one.

I’ve been trying to avoid using LLMs (though I will not get into that because I am exhausted by LLM discourse and I’m sure you are too), but I really had no idea how to figure out what the battery was so I asked an LLM. It gave the response “LIR2477”, which (when I looked it up) looked exactly the same as my battery so I figured that was plausible.

I would be interested to learn non-LLM ways to figure this out though. There must be a way. Lauria showed me how to use DigiKey’s search which was very cool though DigiKey didn’t have that part.

step 6: buy the battery

I went to AliExpress and ordered:

  1. 2 batteries (I had 2 bike lights and I wanted to fix them both)
  2. some silicone glue to glue things back together

I think the batteries were $3 each and the glue was $8.

step 7: solder the new batteries in and glue it back together

The parts took maybe 2 weeks to arive, and once they arrived, I went back to the makerspace and:

  • soldered in the new batteries
  • put the screws back in. The screws were very small and hard to hold, so at this point I dropped some screws on the ground and couldn’t find them because they were too small. So I just used fewer screws and hoped for the best.
  • used the glue to try to put everything back together.
  • Make a somewhat halfhearted attempt to clamp the parts I was gluing together

Then after waiting some amount of time for the glue to dry I took it home and waited 24 hours for the glue to cure.

Also I took the old batteries to somewhere nearby that accepts old batteries.

it works!

The lights work! I have used them to bike at night! I still haven’t needed to recharge them (and tragically I had to order a new Mini USB cable because I got rid of all my Mini USB cables, so I’m still waiting for that), so I still don’t know for sure how long the lifetime of the new battery will be.

Here’s what the light looks like after re-gluing. You can see that I didn’t glue very carefully. It didn’t really go back together that well but I’m hoping it’ll be good enough.

I thought it was really cool that I was able to do this with extremely minimal electronics skills! It cost about $20 CAD to buy the parts, and (whether or not the repair holds up, I’ll try to update this post in the future!), it was fun to try to repair something and learn something new.

I tried to recharge them, but after fully charging them, they only worked for maybe 5 minutes before they turned off again.

title: The Lowball Delusion: How DFW Homeowners Keep Willingly Handing Their Life Savings to Remodeling Scammers
description:
The Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex is currently overflowing with two things: absurd amounts of unearned home equity and a seemingly bottomless supply of gullible homeowners who genuinely believe a full kitchen overhaul, master bath remodel, and second-story addition can be executed flawlessly for thirty grand by a guy named “Chad” they met on Instagram. Welcome to the Golden Age of DFW remodeling fraud, where naive residents act shocked—shocked!—when the absolute lowest bidder turns out to be a career grifter who wrecks their house, steals their money, and vanishes into thin air.   If you think that sounds overly cynical, allow me to introduce you to Christopher and Raquelle Judge of Judge DFW LLC. As detailed in federal court filings from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas and reported by local outlets like WFAA News, this dynamic duo managed to fleece over forty North Texas families out of nearly five million dollars. Their business model was magnificently simple: flash some pretty rendering software on social media, claim to be a licensed architect when you’re absolutely not, collect massive upfront checks, do just enough destructive demolition to render the house totally uninhabitable, and then divert the cash into luxury cars, private school tuition, and plastic surgery. While dozens of homeowners were forced to live in campers over the holidays, the Judges were literally getting cosmetic procedures using their clients’ framing budgets.   How does a disaster of this scale happen so routinely in our area? Because in the Great State of Texas, consumer protection in residential construction is an absolute joke. The state mandates strict state licensing for hairdressers, manicurists, and massage therapists, but if you want to tear out load-bearing walls and re-wire a 200-amp electrical panel, all you need is a leased F-150, a magnet logo for the door, and zero conscience. Texas requires precisely zero general contractor licensing at the state level. Any convicted felon or failed used-car salesman can wake up on Monday morning, declare themselves a “master craftsman,” and start taking deposit checks from eager suburbanites desperate for a bargain.   As I have pounded into readers’ heads for years regarding the infamous “vanishing building code,” the scam almost always starts right there on paper. Shady contractors deliberately wipe any reference to actual building standards—like the International Residential Code—clean out of their contracts. Instead, they write in warm, fuzzy, completely meaningless garbage promising that “work will be performed in a good and workmanlike manner.” What does “workmanlike” mean? It means whatever the guy holding the hammer claims it means on any given Tuesday. Without explicit, legally binding code requirements baked directly into the agreement, you have zero leverage when your brand-new shower drains backwards into your hallway closet.   The deception deepens before a single tool even touches your drywall. Most of these fly-by-night operators aren’t even registered as contractors in the cities where they operate, meaning they couldn’t legally pull a building permit if they tried. So what do they do? They put on their best trustworthy face and start spinning fairy tales to convince you that permits are a big, scary mistake. They’ll tell you that pulling a permit “just slows down the job with government bureaucracy” or, my personal favorite, “it will alert the county tax assessor and double your property taxes overnight.” It’s an absolute line of crap. What they are actually saying is: “Please don’t let anyone with a clipboard see the fire hazards I’m building in your new kitchen.”   And for the love of sanity, stop believing that a municipal building permit is your knight in shining armor. As I’ve explained in my guides on navigating Texas building codes, a city building inspector is not your personal concierge or quality assurance manager. They are overworked city employees who pull up to your driveway, glance out the window for forty-five seconds to make sure your house isn’t actively collapsing onto the sidewalk, drop off a green tag, and zoom off to their next thirty appointments. A city sign-off means you achieved the absolute bare minimum standard required by law to avoid immediate code enforcement—it does not mean your contractor installed your flashings correctly or built anything worth paying for.   When the project inevitably collapses into chaos, homeowners suddenly discover that the legal system is stacked entirely against them. Bad contractors love hiding behind Chapter 27 of the Texas Property Code—the infamous Residential Construction Liability Act—and mandatory arbitration clauses buried in their boilerplate contracts. These clauses are designed to trap you in an endless, soul-crushing cycle of legal notices, cure periods, and private arbitration fees that will drain your remaining life savings before you ever get a day in court. By the time you realize you’ve been taken, the contractor has already dissolved their LLC, formed a brand-new one under a slightly different name, and bought another jet ski or just moved to another state to start the scamming anew.   This shameless grift reaches a fever pitch every time a hail cell rolls through DFW. Within twenty-four hours, a swarm of out-of-state storm-chasers descends upon your neighborhood offering to “absorb,” “waive,” or “rebate” your insurance deductible. The Texas Department of Insurance warns people about this constantly, because it explicitly violates Section 27.02 of the Texas Business and Commerce Code. title: Pabellón El Eco 2020: Cronoboros / TANAT
description: Through the Manifesto of Emotional Architecture (published in 1953), Mathias Goeritz expressed a new form of architecture that goes beyond a logical and rational understanding of space, opening up the possibility of creating buildings capable of evoking deep sensations. As an exemplar of this architecture, Goeritz conceived the El Eco museum as an experiment liberated from classical standards and criteria such as symmetry, structural coherence, and even the way space is inhabited through a specific and unique function for each area. In doing so, reintroducing emotion to architecture revives the possibility of conceiving it as part of a complex system of arts: sculpture, painting, dance, music, poetry, and architecture integrated into a single unity.

Their results were consistent with an overdiagnosis rate below 5%, rather than estimates approaching 30% to 50%.

title: The Full Moon / SHISUO design office
description: Invited by the Power Station of Art (PSA), SHISUO Design Office has unveiled "The Full Moon" an urban public art installation celebrating the Mid-Autumn Festival in Shanghai. The installation was realized in collaboration with Shi Qinling, a Shanghai-style paper-cutting inheritor, and is themed around the moon, rabbits, and the art of paper-cutting. Across various cultures, the rabbit holds a unique place in the human imagination as one of the few animal figures beloved by all. In China's classical Mid-Autumn folklore, the rabbit is a constant companion to the moon—the moon symbolizes the cyclical waxing and waning of existence, while the rabbit metaphorically represents the vitality, growth, and flourishing of all beings.

title: El Niño fuels Pacific storms as Atlantic lacks hurricanes
description:
An exceptionally strong El Niño is driving sharply different hurricane seasons in the Pacific and Atlantic. By Sept. 25, the Pacific had recorded 41 named storms, including 18 hurricanes, while the Atlantic had produced no hurricanes [npr.org#1]. Scientists cited El Niño as a key reason for the contrast [npr.org#1][abcnews.com#1].

Hurricane Polo rapidly intensified off Mexico, while Hurricane Nolo strengthened south of Hawaii. Nolo threatened the Big Island with extreme rain, flash flooding and mudslides. Forecasts called for 15 to 30 inches of rain in parts of the Big Island, with higher local totals possible; Nolo was not expected to make landfall [nasa.gov#1][earthsky.org#1][gpb.org#1][koaa.com#1].

title: Banks and Credit Unions to Team Up Against Apple Pay Fees
description:
An antitrust lawsuit accusing Apple of blocking tap-to-pay competition is moving forward and will see banks and credit unions able to band together to sue Apple.


U.S. District Judge Jeffrey White this week certified a class in the lawsuit. It will include any U.S. entities that issued any payment card enabled for Apple Pay and paid Apple a fee for ‌Apple Pay‌ transactions on that payment card. He also denied a motion from Apple to exclude expert testimony that plaintiff attorneys allege offers proof Apple has monopoly power over the mobile wallet market.

First filed in 2022, the suit claims Apple illegally collects up to $1 billion annually in fees by preventing rivals from accessing the iPhone's NFC chip to build mobile wallets that would compete with ‌Apple Pay‌. When an iPhone user buys something with a card linked to ‌Apple Pay‌, the card issuer has to pay Apple a 0.15 percent fee for credit cards and half a cent for debit cards, according to the lawsuit. If you make a $1,000 purchase via ‌Apple Pay‌, Apple collects $1.50 from the card issuer.

The complaint alleges that Apple forces card issuers to pay fees by making ‌Apple Pay‌ the only tap-to-pay option. It points to Google's Android, which supports multiple wallets and does not collect a fee from card issuers for contactless payments. It suggests Apple would not be able to continue to charge "substantial fees" if it were forced to support other mobile wallets on Apple devices.

Apple has changed its policies since the lawsuit was filed. As of iOS 18.1, developers are able to offer NFC contactless payments in their apps. Developers have access to the NFC chip in the United States, Canada, Australia, Brazil, Japan, New Zealand, the UK, the European Economic Area, and many other countries.

Attorneys are seeking repayment of the fees card issuers have paid and injunctive relief to "put an end to Apple's policies."

Related Forum: Apple Music, Apple Pay/Card, iCloud, Fitness+

title: Workers are faking their interest in AI to satisfy bosses, report shows
description:
Corporate leaders are putting tremendous pressure on workers to incorporate artificial intelligence into their workflow—often without a clear understanding of its capabilities or impact. As a result, some employees are simply faking their usage of AI. 

According to a new report by Vancouver-based software firm Visier, nearly half of workers (48%) said they have “exaggerated their AI usage or expertise to colleagues or leadership” to keep up with expectations. 

Visier polled 1,000 full-time workers in the United States—across healthcare, finance, human resources, and other domains—about how they use AI and their opinion on their firm’s AI strategy. 

The survey found that while AI has had a real impact on many workers—54% of respondents said their roles or careers had “significantly changed due to AI in the past two years”—the nature of its impact varied widely from worker to worker. Some said AI has improved their job performance and satisfaction, while others reported that its impact was mostly negative. 

Anxiety and uncertainty caused by AI were widespread. Nearly 60% said they are unsure of their employer’s plan to address changes brought on by AI, and 45% said they felt pressured to use AI “even when they’re not confident in how to use it effectively.”

The pressure to use AI leads some workers to pretend they are using it even when they aren’t, believing that showing enthusiasm for AI matters just as much (or more than) getting better results. 

Indeed, the report concludes that the underlying driver of “performative AI use” is a lack of trust in leadership. Nearly a third (32%) of respondents told Visier they want “more AI training and upskilling opportunities,” while 31% called for “greater transparency” on AI-related issues. 

Simply telling workers to “have AI do it” isn’t going to cut it—they must be told how. Along with resisting the pull of AI FOMO, leaders should listen to employees’ concerns, stay transparent about how AI might affect their work, and provide the necessary training. 

“By providing employees with opportunities to upskill, learn, and share knowledge among colleagues, leaders can proactively prevent performative AI behaviors and help alleviate workforce anxiety,” the report states.

title: The FDA approved the new mFlusiva flu vaccine, but the CDC isn’t recommending it. Here’s why
description:
The Food and Drug Administration recently approved a new flu vaccine that tested well in older adults. But the federal agency responsible for telling doctors and the general public how to use it has made no recommendation on it.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s inaction on the mFlusiva vaccine marks a break in longstanding practice. It’s also an example of how the agency’s vaccine review-and-recommendation process has been blown up in the past year, grinding decision-making to a halt.

Efforts by vaccine-wary officials in President Donald Trump’s administration to scale back shot recommendations have been put on hold. Federal guidance on new vaccines has stopped. And public discussion of vaccine policy questions that might cross political divides — including whether there’s solid evidence to justify giving fewer shots to kids — has diminished.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s crusade to upend vaccine policy and the legal action opposing it have disrupted longstanding systems that deliver crucial health guidance to Americans, affecting whether people are getting the best available protection against vaccine-preventable diseases.

“We find ourselves at a point where even if credible evidence (for a new vaccine policy) has reached a tipping point, we don’t have an obvious mechanism that can formalize that change,” said Jason Schwartz, a Yale University health policy researcher who studies government health agencies.

Many in the medical field praised a court ruling that halted Kennedy’s changes

For 60 years, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices guided the CDC’s vaccine recommendations. The committee met publicly, reviewed vaccine data and sought input from various health groups. The panel voted on recommendations that went to the CDC director, who almost always adopted them as the government’s guidance, leading public and private insurers to pay for the shots.

Trump, a Republican, appointed Kennedy to oversee federal health agencies, including the CDC. Kennedy last year dismissed the committee and replaced it with a group that included several anti-vaccine voices. Controversial decisions followed, leading to a lawsuit from the American Academy of Pediatrics and some other medical groups.

In March, a federal judge said Kennedy likely violated federal procedures, stopped Kennedy’s panel from holding further meetings and suspended Kennedy’s decision to reduce the number of vaccines recommended for children.

Many in the medical and public health communities celebrated the decision and took the order as a respite from what they saw as the Trump administration’s assault on vaccines.

Dr. Jason Goldman, president of the American College of Physicians, said he hoped “it will mean a return to a transparent and evidence-driven process that safeguards the health of all communities and the best interests of our patients.”

In reality, the process stalled and splintered

With Kennedy’s committee shut down by the court order, doctors’ groups that used to collaborate with the ACIP have gone their own way. Working with a University of Minnesota researcher, they have debated — not publicly — the kind of medical evidence formerly presented at ACIP meetings and issued their own recommendations.

The trade association for private health insurers decided to heed the medical societies’ choices, and the insurers have continued to pay for shots recommended by those organizations.

Many of the groups’ recommendations match prior ones made by ACIP and the CDC before Kennedy’s arrival. But they also made their own updates.

For example, ACIP previously recommended that a new shot be given to women late in pregnancy: a vaccine against respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, which can be dangerous to newborns. The government panel recommended that the vaccine be given between September and January in most of the U.S., to coincide with the time of year when RSV infections are most common.

But RSV season sometimes remains active longer. For that reason, the medical groups recently said the shot should be offered to those women through the beginning of March.

“We all recognized this needs to evolve,” Chris Regal, director of clinical innovation at America’s Health Insurance Plans, the health insurance trade association, said in a recent webinar.

The official CDC guidance remains unchanged.

Unanswered vaccine issues are piling up

The mFlusiva flu shot is another example of the unusual way vaccine policy updates have stalled.

The shot is the first flu vaccine made with the mRNA technology that was key to ending the COVID-19 pandemic. Kennedy has criticized mRNA vaccines and last year canceled contracts for the development of new ones. The shots also took a tortuous path through the FDA, which finally granted full approval in people ages 50 to 64.

But the CDC this month quietly posted that it has decided to maintain its flu vaccine endorsements from last year due to “legal uncertainties and inquiries.” That means mFlusiva is not among the listed flu vaccines recommended to the public this fall.
The medical societies are recommending it as an option, however.

Another ACIP function was to vote on whether certain vaccines should be covered by Vaccines for Children, a government program that pays for shots for children who have no health insurance.

The FDA approved updated COVID-19 vaccines, but as the summer dragged on — and fall vaccination campaigns got underway — the government would not say if the VFC program will pay for those shots. It was only this week that officials confirmed orders could be placed through that program.

HPV vaccine reassessment is derailed

Another question concerns the HPV vaccine, given to preteens to prevent certain cancers.

Two HPV shots are recommended, but some recent research has suggested that perhaps one shot could be enough — at least for girls. Indeed, in 2024 the ACIP formed a working group to begin a reassessment of the recommendations.

That work was derailed when Kennedy fired the entire committee. In January, he decided on his own to order that the number of recommended doses be reduced to one as part of a dramatic contraction of the childhood vaccination schedule. His decision was suspended by the judge’s order.

Experts are trying to better understand the timing and the duration of protection from just one dose, particularly in boys. The American Academy of Pediatrics is weighing a change to its HPV vaccination recommendations and could reach a conclusion later this year, said the AAP’s Dr. James Campbell.

It’s possible that the medical societies will end up agreeing with Kennedy on just how many HPV shots make sense. But that might not necessarily clear up the current mess, Schwartz said.

“The credibility of the Trump administration, when it comes to vaccine recommendations, is so compromised in the eyes of the mainstream medical and public health communities,” he said, “that even recommendations that might align with where the public health community was trending are likely to be viewed with skepticism or distrust.”

Meanwhile, the Trump administration is considering changing the federal government’s categories for vaccine recommendations, although a specific proposal has not been released and a Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson did not respond to questions about what is being contemplated. Public comments were due earlier this week.

An alliance of 15 Democratic state governors said the proposed changes are likely to increase confusion and administrative complexity.

“It’s Governors and their residents who bear the brunt of any increased disease outbreaks due to confusion related to hastily made federal changes,” Angela Botticella, managing director of the Governors Public Health Alliance, said in a statement.

title: Best iPhone 2026: Every iPhone compared
description:
Macworld

Apple’s 2026 iPhone lineup is broader than ever, ranging from the relatively affordable iPhone 17e to the high-end iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, plus the ultra-thin iPhone Air and the new folding iPhone Duo. That gives buyers more choice, but it also makes picking the right model more complicated than simply choosing the newest or most expensive iPhone.

For most people, the iPhone 17 is the best all-round choice, thanks to its 6.3-inch ProMotion display, strong battery life, dual 48MP cameras and 256GB of storage as standard. The iPhone 17e is the better option if price matters most, while the iPhone 18 Pro is the model to choose for the best cameras and performance. The iPhone 18 Pro Max adds the longest battery life, the iPhone Air prioritises thinness and low weight, and the iPhone Duo offers Apple’s biggest and most flexible display.

Which iPhone is best for you will therefore depend on what you value most. Camera enthusiasts should look closely at the Pro models, heavy users may prefer the Pro Max for its battery life, while parents, older users and anyone trying to keep costs down may find the 17e a much better fit. There can also be excellent value in buying a discounted or refurbished older iPhone rather than paying full price for the latest hardware.

This guide focuses on the best iPhone to buy for different types of user and budget. If you want to dig deeper into the differences between every model, see our complete iPhone Buying Guide, where we compare the cameras, displays, performance, storage, battery life and other key specifications across Apple’s current lineup.

Which iPhone to buy: At a glance

1. Apple iPhone 17 – Best iPhone for most people

Pros

  • Excellent overall value
  • ProMotion Always-On display
  • Dual 48MP cameras

Cons

  • No dedicated telephoto
  • Limited to 512GB
Price When Reviewed: $899 (was $799)
Best Prices Today:
Retailer
Price
Check
Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide

Why we recommend it

The iPhone 17 brings several features previously reserved for Pro models to Apple’s mainstream iPhone, including a 120Hz ProMotion display and Always-On support. It also offers the fast A19 chip, dual 48MP cameras, an improved Centre Stage selfie camera, strong battery life and 256GB of storage as standard. For most buyers, it strikes the best balance between price and features.

Buy iPhone 17 if

Buy the iPhone 17 if you want the best all-round iPhone without paying Pro prices. Its 6.3-inch ProMotion display, excellent cameras, strong battery life and 256GB starting storage make it particularly appealing to anyone upgrading from an iPhone 14 or older.

Don’t buy iPhone 17 if

Don’t buy it if you want optical zoom beyond 2x or Apple’s most advanced camera features—in that case, choose the iPhone 18 Pro. The iPhone Air is a better choice if thinness and low weight are your priorities, while existing iPhone 16 owners may find the upgrade relatively modest unless ProMotion and improved battery life are particularly important.

What do you get that you don’t get with the iPhone 17e?

For the extra $200, the iPhone 17 gives you a larger 6.3-inch ProMotion Always-On display, Dynamic Island, a second 48MP Ultra Wide camera with macro photography, a brighter screen, stronger graphics performance, a better 18MP Centre Stage selfie camera and longer battery life. For most people who can afford the difference, it’s money well spent.

What do you get that you don’t get with the iPhone 16?

Which iPhone has the best camera? iPhone 18 Pro

Apple

The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max have the best camera systems of any current iPhone. Both models use the same triple-48MP rear camera setup, so there is no photographic advantage to choosing the larger Pro Max unless you also want its bigger display and longer battery life.

The headline upgrade is the 48MP Main camera with variable aperture, which gives photographers more control over depth of field and should improve low-light performance. The Pro models also include a 48MP Ultra Wide camera and a 48MP Telephoto camera with 4x and 8x optical-quality zoom, giving them far more flexibility than Apple’s cheaper iPhones.

The standard iPhone 17 is still an excellent camera phone, with 48MP Main and Ultra Wide cameras, plus an improved 18MP Centre Stage front camera. For everyday photography it will be more than enough for most people, but it lacks the dedicated telephoto lens, longer zoom and advanced video features of the Pro models.

The iPhone Duo is more compromised. Despite its premium price, it has only two 48MP rear cameras and lacks a dedicated telephoto camera, variable aperture, ProRes and Apple Log. Its strengths are instead its fold-specific shooting features and dual-screen flexibility.

The iPhone Air and iPhone 17e are the least versatile, with just a single 48MP rear camera.

Our choice: If photography and video are your priority, buy the iPhone 18 Pro. It offers the same camera system as the Pro Max for less money and in a more manageable size.

Which iPhone has the best battery life? iPhone 18 Pro Max

Apple

The iPhone 18 Pro Max has the best battery life of any current iPhone, with Apple rating it for up to 45 hours of video playback. That puts it comfortably ahead of the smaller iPhone 18 Pro and makes battery life one of the strongest reasons to choose the Pro Max.

The iPhone Duo comes surprisingly close, with up to 44 hours of video playback when using its outer 5.4-inch display. However, battery life drops to around 31 hours when using the larger 7.6-inch folding display, so the Pro Max remains the better choice if endurance is your priority.

The iPhone 18 Pro is also excellent, offering up to 36 hours of video playback. That makes it a good compromise if you want strong battery life without carrying the much larger and heavier Pro Max.

Further down the range, the iPhone 17 offers up to 30 hours, making it the best mainstream option for battery life. The iPhone Air manages around 27 hours despite its exceptionally thin design, while the iPhone 17e reaches 26 hours.

The older iPhone 16 trails the current lineup at up to 22 hours of video playback.

Our choice: If battery life matters above everything else, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is the clear winner. Its combination of a 45-hour rating, huge 6.9-inch display and Pro-level performance makes it particularly well suited to heavy users, travellers and anyone who wants to get through a long day without worrying about charging.

Here’s how the current iPhone lineup compares in terms of battery life

What is the best value iPhone? iPhone 17

Hannah Cowton-Barnes / Foundry

The iPhone 17 offers the best overall value for money in Apple’s current lineup. The iPhone 17e is cheaper, but the extra $200/£200 for the iPhone 17 buys a surprisingly large number of worthwhile upgrades.

You get a larger 6.3-inch 120Hz ProMotion display with Always-On support and Dynamic Island, rather than the 17e’s standard 60Hz 6.1-inch screen. The iPhone 17 also adds a second 48MP Ultra Wide camera, including macro photography, along with a better 18MP Centre Stage front camera.

Battery life is stronger too, at up to 30 hours of video playback, compared with 26 hours on the iPhone 17e. You also get stronger graphics performance and a more premium overall experience, while both phones start with a generous 256GB of storage.

At $799/£799, the iPhone 17 also compares very favourably with the older iPhone 16. For just $100/£100 more, you get double the base storage, ProMotion, a larger and brighter display, improved cameras, the newer A19 chip and significantly better battery life.

If your priority is spending as little as possible, choose the iPhone 17e which delivers excellent performance for $599/£599. Or seek out a refurbished iPhone from the Apple Refurbished Store or another place that sells refurbished iPhones.

Our choice: In terms of the features and hardware you get for every pound or dollar spent, the iPhone 17 is the sweet spot. For most buyers, it delivers the best balance of price, performance, cameras, display quality, battery life and longevity without paying for Pro-level features they may never use. Even better if you can find a iPhone 17 deal, then you are really getting a bargain.

Best iPhone for gaming: iPhone 18 Pro

Foundry

The iPhone 18 Pro is the best iPhone for gaming for most people, thanks to its combination of the A20 Pro chip, seven-core GPU and improved vapor-chamber cooling.

The A20 Pro is Apple’s fastest iPhone processor, but the cooling system is just as important for gaming. Better heat management should help the iPhone 18 Pro maintain high performance for longer during demanding games, rather than slowing down as the phone gets hot. Its 6.3-inch 120Hz ProMotion display also provides smooth animation and responsive gameplay without making the phone excessively large or heavy.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max offers essentially the same gaming performance, but adds a much larger 6.9-inch display and significantly longer battery life. That arguably makes it the best choice for serious mobile gamers who value screen size and endurance, although it is heavier and costs more.

The iPhone Duo also uses the A20 Pro and has an enormous 7.6-inch folding display, which could be fantastic for some games, but its weight, price and unconventional form factor make it a more specialised choice.

Our choice: For most gamers, the iPhone 18 Pro offers the best balance of performance, cooling, display quality and portability. It’s the best choice if you prefer a more pocketable device but still want top-tier gaming power.

Best iPhone for seniors and older users: iPhone 17e

David Price / Foundry

For most older users, the iPhone 17e is probably the best choice, because it combines a relatively simple feature set with modern performance, strong battery life and a lower price than Apple’s flagship models.

Its 6.1-inch OLED display is large enough to make text, icons and controls easy to see without making the phone too bulky, while the A19 chip should keep it feeling fast for years. It also supports Apple Intelligence and starts with 256GB of storage, so there’s plenty of room for photos, apps and videos.

The iPhone 17 is a better option for someone who would benefit from a larger and more advanced display. Its 6.3-inch ProMotion screen, Always-On support and higher brightness can make scrolling, reading and outdoor use more comfortable. It also offers stronger battery life and better cameras, although it costs more.

We don’t recommend the iPhone Air, Pro Max or Duo for older users. The Air sacrifices battery life and camera flexibility for thinness, while the Pro Max and Duo are much heavier and considerably more expensive.

Our choice: iPhone 17e is the perfect choice for most older users.

Best iPhone for kids: iPhone 17e

Ida Blix

The iPhone 17e is the best iPhone for most children. As Apple’s most affordable current-generation model, it offers the best balance of price, performance and longevity, while being easier to justify than a flagship model if it gets lost or damaged.

It uses the same A19 chip as the iPhone 17, albeit with one fewer GPU core, so it’s easily fast enough for games, social media, schoolwork and Apple Intelligence. Battery life is strong, the 6.1-inch OLED display is a sensible size for smaller hands, and the 48MP camera is more than capable for everyday photos, even though it lacks an Ultra Wide lens.

The iPhone 17 is the better choice for older teenagers who care more about photography, video or display quality. It adds a 48MP Ultra Wide camera, a better front camera and a larger 6.3-inch ProMotion display, but costs considerably more.

A hand-me-down iPhone is also worth considering. It’s the cheapest option and better for the environment, provided you erase the phone first, create a Child Account through Family Sharing, and configure Screen Time and parental controls before handing it over. Read: How to set up an iPhone for a child.

Whichever iPhone you choose, those controls matter. In iOS 27, Apple is expanding Screen Time with new category-based Time Allowances, Ask to Browse, more flexible app schedules and improved contact controls. Communication Safety can also detect and blur sensitive, violent or graphic content.

For very young children, an iPad may still be a better first Apple device. By the time they reach 11 or 12 though, an iPhone becomes much more useful for staying in touch.

Our choice: iPhone 17e for most kids; iPhone 17 for older teens who want better cameras and display quality.

Should you buy an older iPhone?

Macwelt

Buying an older iPhone can be a great way to save money, but the key is choosing a model that still has plenty of useful life ahead of it. Apple typically provides around five to seven years of major iOS updates, with security updates often continuing for longer, so a relatively recent iPhone can remain perfectly usable for years.

We wouldn’t recommend simply buying the cheapest iPhone you can find. Very old models may technically run recent versions of iOS, but performance, battery condition and access to newer features can become increasingly compromised. We currently recommend avoiding anything older than the iPhone 15 Pro because even the iPhone 15 doesn’t support Apple Intelligence. You should definitely avoid models such as the iPhone XS and XR that can no longer run the latest iOS releases.

A refurbished recent-generation iPhone can offer particularly good value. You may be able to buy a former Pro model with better cameras and displays for less than a new entry-level iPhone. Buying from a reputable refurbisher is important, however: check the warranty, battery condition, returns policy and whether genuine replacement parts have been used. Apple’s own refurbished iPhones include a new battery and outer shell and come with a one-year warranty.

Our advice: A discounted or refurbished iPhone 16 or newer should offer an excellent combination of price, features and longevity.

title: Résidence Lourmel / MARS Architectes
description: Built on a former parking ramp, the Lourmel student housing is conceived as an intermediate figure between the existing buildings and the central garden. Rather than creating a continuous volume, it is divided into four slightly offset blocks. Their shifts and rotations respond to constraints of distance, views and privacy, while opening diagonal perspectives, improving daylight and strengthening connections to the landscape. The volumes gradually recede towards the center of the block, creating a more porous relationship with the street. The existing courtyard is also fully re-landscaped.

The intervention combines the existing structure with new timber elements, an energy retrofit, and the transformation of the former asphalt courtyard into a permeable green space.

title: A strong El Niño actually means fewer Atlantic hurricanes, but the Pacific has been extra stormy
description:
The Atlantic Ocean has had an unusually quiet hurricane season this year. While six named storms have formed, not a single one has strengthened into a hurricane—a rarity that hasn’t occurred in decades.

On the other side of the country, though, Hurricane Polo has rapidly intensified, becoming one of the most intense eastern Pacific hurricanes on record.

These weather anomalies may seem at odds, but they’re both impacted by the “Godzilla” Super El Niño that experts say is shaping up to be one of the strongest in history. 

El Niño affects weather patterns around the world, and can amplify extreme weather events. And even though El Niño may reduce the number of hurricanes in the Atlantic, that doesn’t always mean the season is less destructive than other years.

It’s late September—where are all the Atlantic hurricanes?

The Atlantic hurricane season spans from June 1 to November 30, though it tends to peak around September 10. In fact, AccuWeather notes that it is unusual “not to have a hurricane spinning on that date.”

On average, a season sees 14 named storms in the Atlantic, with seven that become hurricanes and three that strengthen into major hurricanes.

By September 24 this year, though, there have still been no hurricanes in that ocean. (Tropical Storm Fay is spinning in the central Atlantic Ocean, but it poses no threat to the United States, experts say.)

“The latest occurrence of the first Atlantic hurricane in the last 100 years was September 21, 1941,” Chad Merrill, a senior meteorologist with AccuWeather, tells Fast Company. “That record is being demolished as we speak.”

“In the entire record of the Atlantic basin, the latest occurrence of the first hurricane was October 7, 1905. It’s yet to be seen if this record is demolished,” he adds. 

Hurricanes need three features to form, the U.S. Geological Survey notes: warm ocean water; warm air at the ocean’s surface that can then cool and rise; and “low wind shear,” or little difference in the wind’s speed and direction within different levels of the atmosphere.

A predominant feature of an El Niño is hotter ocean water in the Pacific. But the phenomenon still affects activity in the Atlantic, too. 

There’s less of a chance of Atlantic hurricanes during El Niño years because of the way it changes winds: Increased wind shear means stronger winds sweeping across the Atlantic, which makes it less likely for storms to form and strengthen. 

El Niño fuels more hurricanes in the Pacific

Across the country, hurricane season looks starkly different.

There have already been 16 named storms and six hurricanes that have formed across the central and eastern Pacific, fueled by El Niño’s warmer waters and lower wind shear there.

Typically, an El Niño means drier-than-normal conditions in the northeastern parts of the U.S., and wetter-than-normal conditions across the South. El Niños also strengthen the Pacific jet stream, a current of air that flows from west to east. 

That stronger jet stream, combined with the hot Pacific Ocean temperatures, can strengthen storms that hit the West Coast of the country.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) predicted that the Pacific hurricane season would be above average, with nine to 14 hurricanes and five to nine major hurricanes in that ocean, fueled by this record-breaking El Niño. 

The latest example of this effect is Hurricane Polo, a Category 4 storm off the southwest coast of Mexico that meteorologists have said is one of the strongest Pacific basin storms on record.

Though that storm is off the coast of Mexico, the strong jet stream could draw moisture north, bringing a “good chance” of flash flooding to New Mexico, Texas, and Oklahoma, Merrill says.

Experts are also warning that Tropical Storm Nolo (not to be confused with Hurricane Polo) in the Pacific could soon be a major hurricane, potentially bringing more than 30 inches of extreme rain to Hawaii’s Big Island.

Super El Niño means all sorts of extreme weather

Though this year’s El Niño may mean fewer Atlantic hurricanes, no one is completely safe from its impacts. While it is a natural phenomenon, this year’s warm ocean temperatures are combining with record-breaking global ocean heat fueled by climate change, creating a particularly strong Godzilla Super El Niño.

It’s not that climate change is directly making the El Niño stronger, climatologist Michael Mann told BCC, but “it’s like a wave that’s on top of a rising tide. . . . Every time we get a large El Niño event like this one, it’s sitting on top of a warmer planet.”

That warmth on top of warmth can supercharge extreme weather everywhere.

“When the oceans are warmer, thanks to climate change and the developing El Niño, they release vast amounts of moisture into the atmosphere, which act as extra fuel for any storm,” Union of Concerned Scientists climate scientist Marc Alessi wrote on BlueSky.

That’s evident through Tropical Storm Nolo, which is being fueled by record ocean heat—as well as an early-season nor’easter developing in the Atlantic, Alessi adds, and the extreme rain in New Mexico. 

El Niño could also bring sharp cold fronts into the Great Lakes and Northeast, AccuWeather’s Merrill notes, and even warm and dry weather to the West, which leads to a higher-than-average fire risk.

In this way, the record-breaking El Niño offers a glimpse into a future where a warmer world fuels extreme weather across the entire planet, in one way or another.

title: Entry-level tech jobs in NYC are being cut in half by the AI boom
description:
At first glance, the tech scene in New York City appears to be thriving: OpenAI and Anthropic have been putting down roots in the city, while stalwarts of the tech industry like Google now have more than 14,000 employees based in New York. Between 2008 and 2023, tech employment in the city has increased 160%, outdone only by the explosive growth of the tech industry in San Francisco.

But overall job growth in NYC’s tech industry has stagnated in recent years, and there is one area in particular that has experienced a sharp dip: Entry-level tech jobs have taken a significant hit in the years since ChatGPT’s public release ushered in the AI boom. 

A new report from the Center for an Urban Future (CUF), a New York-based think tank, found that as of 2022, the number of entry-level job postings in the tech industry has dropped 49%—a bigger decline than in any other sector, even as generative AI has seemingly derailed entry-level hiring across sectors. There continues to be a steady supply of college graduates with computer science degrees, but there aren’t nearly enough entry-level positions available to them. 

“The core issue is that employers face an individual incentive to hire workers who already have two or three years of experience,” Eli Dvorkin, editorial and policy director at CUF and one of the authors of the report, said in a recent interview with Searchlight. “But if every employer acts that way, the broader entry-level ecosystem collapses, which ultimately harms employers as well.”

The analysis found that on the whole, the jobs that have seen a marked dip in hiring are those that are most exposed to generative AI. Since 2022, entry-level job postings in roles with high AI exposure have decreased 29% across New York City. 

The outlook is not quite as grim across other jobs: Entry-level hiring has remained robust—growing 21%—for jobs that are not especially exposed to AI, according to the CUF report. Even within tech, employers have continued hiring for roles that require expertise in security and data analysis. Entry-level workers with strong AI skills are in particularly high demand, and job postings have actually climbed 20% in over the past four years. 

Still, the overall decline in hiring for entry-level tech jobs echoes a broader shift in New York: Since 2022, most industries have seen a steady drop in job postings for entry-level roles. 

This hiring slump is representative of a broader phenomenon playing out across the country, particularly in sectors like tech and finance. Some economists have been wary about overstating the impact of generative AI on the labor force—and even high-profile AI leaders have walked back their bold claims about AI ushering in widespread job losses. 

But there are clear signs that entry-level workers are bearing the brunt of the toll: Stanford University’s Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence recently found that the employment gap for young workers (defined as workers ages 22 to 25) has widened in the last year to 19%, when compared against similarly situated workers in roles that are less exposed to AI. 

In a recent survey by the Pew Research Center, young workers were more skeptical of AI than they had been previously, a sign that they are increasingly concerned about how the fast-developing technology might upend the labor market. Nearly three-quarters of adults younger than 30 said they believe AI will reduce the number of jobs within the next two decades.

The reports of looming job losses often focus on how generative AI is impacting white-collar workers, but research from the Brookings Institution earlier this year indicates that it’s not just highly skilled candidates who are being shut out of the workforce. AI adoption is also disrupting the pathways available to people without college degrees who have traditionally been able to move into white-collar work. 

In cities like New York, the growth in tech employment has in the past helped many workers from low-income backgrounds move into more lucrative jobs—but the changes ushered in by AI may make it more difficult for those types of workers to find their footing. Those pathways could disappear altogether if the city doesn’t reinvest in its tech workforce and help New Yorkers get the experience they need to land the entry-level jobs that are in high demand. 

As Dvorkin put it recently: “If anything, our tech sector has proven remarkably resilient given all these macroeconomic changes and technology shifts, and it remains well-positioned for future growth. However, the real challenge is who gets the opportunity to enter that sector in the first place.”

title: Executives are using AI to communicate better. There’s just one problem
description:
Artificial intelligence can help executives communicate more effectively and efficiently. But relying on it too much carries significant risks. 

One of the biggest is something Wade Foster, cofounder and chief executive of workflow automation platform Zapier, calls the “comprehension gap”—failing to adequately understand the underlying subject matter of their own AI-assisted work. 

Leaders who overuse AI to write polished memos, emails, or talking points may find themselves unable to answer follow-up questions or back up their claims in real time. The fact that they used AI to create the original material might quickly become obvious. 

“There are definitely situations [where] you don’t use AI responsibly, where you’re delegating too much,” Foster said in an appearance on Harvard Business Review’s IdeaCast earlier today.  

“As you get asked questions, as you start to investigate, you realize, ‘Oh, I don’t actually know enough about this area,’” he said. 

AI overuse can also rob executives of knowledge they would have gained by producing the materials themselves, added Matt Abrahams, a lecturer in organizational behavior at Stanford Graduate School of Business. Composing an internal memo about a regulatory issue, for example, might give an executive a deeper understanding of the issue itself. 

“Communication is operationalized critical thinking,” Abrahams said on the IdeaCast podcast. “If we outsource that critical thinking and then are put on the spot to answer questions, to give input, to give an update, people get really anxious.” 

The key to avoiding such a scenario is to take time studying the AI-generated material until you really comprehend it, Abrahams said. It’s about truly knowing the subject matter, even if you had some help putting the verbiage together.

“It is really important not just to review the output, but to really review the thinking so that when you’re put on the spot, you have the confidence that you know what you’re speaking about,” he said. Otherwise, workers might come to believe that their leaders aren’t doing their homework. 

The business community is still figuring how to responsibly incorporate AI into communications, Foster added. “AI is a fantastic tool, and to not use it would be a mistake. [But] it could be a lot better if you use it responsibly. [That] is what everyone’s trying to figure out.” 

Leaders who overuse AI without understanding the underlying subject matter risk their own credibility—one recent study found that employees view executive communications as less helpful when they think they’re AI-generated (even when they aren’t)—and set a bad example for workers who may be eager to outsource their own work to AI.   

In the end, it may be that there are no hard-and-fast rules for responsible AI use in executive communications. Leaders will have to decide on a case-by-case basis. 

“It just depends on the task,” Foster said. “There could be areas where the impact is relatively low, and you’re fine delegating the work to the AI more fully. 

“It just comes down to judgment.”

title: CISA issues election infrastructure security plan 40 days before midterms
description:
The nation’s cybersecurity agency on Thursday released an election infrastructure security plan 40 days before November’s midterms, laying out potential threats to election systems and listing services it would offer to election officials to protect the vote.

The plan, which Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had originally promised to release by mid-August, comes after the Trump administration has been trying to kick-start efforts to help states protect voting systems. Election officials have argued that such efforts are too little, too late after the Trump administration gutted the agency’s election security work last year, forcing the officials to pay for private services to ensure they were prepared for the upcoming elections.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is housed under the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), has since its founding in 2018 helped warn state and local election officials about potential threats from foreign governments.

But CISA, as it’s known, was largely absent from that role in last year’s elections after the Trump administration dismantled much of its role on election security. The administration cut some 1,000 employees from CISA and slashed $10 million from two cybersecurity initiatives, including one dedicated to helping state and local election officials.

CISA has also gone the entirety of Trump’s second term without a Senate-confirmed director, instead cycling through a series of acting leaders.

The 13-page document released Thursday says DHS has “consistently supported CISA’s delivery of cybersecurity and physical security services to election officials,” and that such services are provided at no cost to state and local election officials at their request.

Numerous state and local election officials around the country have told The Associated Press otherwise, noting that services previously provided by CISA, like tabletop exercises and penetration tests to evaluate the security of their systems, were not available in the lead-up to this year’s midterm elections.

—By Ali Swenson, Associated Press

title: As the coding boom fades, AI is forcing colleges and computer science grads to adjust
description:
Computer science student Jack Zemke was getting nowhere despite sending out hundreds of job applications that mostly disappeared into the void—ignored.

With his graduation from Tulane University just days away, he was considering moving back in with his parents when he got a break, thanks to a group project he had worked on involving an AI-powered search tool. As he touted it at an engineering conference, an employee at a civil engineering firm approached.

“We’re not, like, the most on top of trends, but we know that AI is becoming a big thing,” he recalled the man saying. “We need somebody to be essentially an evangelist.”

Zemke responded: “I’m your man.”

It has been a difficult job market for new graduates, especially in fields like software development where artificial intelligence is shouldering more of the work. While college students majoring in computer science during the recent coding boom were getting job offers without even applying, graduates today in philosophy, art history, and ethnic studies majors all have higher employment rates.

But as the job market evolves with AI and entry-level jobs become harder to find, students and schools are adapting. Colleges are experimenting with business-specific internships and bolstering training in AI tools. Schools say most graduates ultimately are getting jobs, although increasingly, the employers hiring aren’t tech giants but smaller businesses looking for help figuring out what to do with AI.

Such was the case with Zemke, 23, who spent a year at the engineering firm before getting hired this summer at an AI tech startup.

“These jobs are expecting you to be able to jump in and kind of operate on the frontier,” Zemke said. “There’s so much churn. People are getting laid off. People are leaving. It really feels like a total frenzy right now.”

A coding boom that enticed many students has fizzled

The elevated jobless rate in the field—at around 7.1% for recent computer science and computer engineering graduates, according to an Associated Press analysis—reflects in part the huge numbers of students who enrolled during the coding boom.

Hiring surged during the pandemic as everything went digital, with software development postings on the job search site Indeed peaking in early 2022.

But now tech giants like Microsoft, Meta, and Google are turning to AI for a larger share of the code writing, and big employers like Amazon are shedding workers as spending on AI accelerates. Far fewer jobs in software development are being posted, according to a Federal Reserve analysis of the Indeed data.

For workers in their early 20s in what are being called “AI-exposed” occupations—such as software development—employment is 19% below where it would be if it had kept pace with employment in fields less exposed to being reshaped by AI, according to the Stanford Digital Economy Lab. The U.S. Census Bureau likened the employment decline to finishing college during a large recession.

What the industry is demanding now is workers who can oversee AI tools and not blindly accept their outputs—skills more common in seasoned workers, said Tracy Camp, the Computing Research Association’s executive director and CEO.

The effect on hiring of young workers is so concerning that the association has reached out to industry leaders, urging them to invest in entry-level workers.

“If they don’t change how hiring is currently happening, they’re not going to have mid-level career people in a few years,” Camp said.

Students also are taking note. After a decade that saw the number of recent computer science and computer engineering graduates triple, to about 362,000 in 2024, enrollment began to drop last year. The latest data from the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center shows that by spring this year, computer and information science enrollment has fallen by 8.4% at four-year institutions.

A shift in hiring disadvantages international students

For international students, who have enrolled in high numbers in computer science programs, it has been an especially challenging job market. Their struggles owe partly to changes to U.S. immigration policy as well as the shift in the kinds of available jobs.

Samir Khuller, the chair of Northwestern University’s computer science department, said many of the smaller companies that are hiring don’t have big human resources departments with experience handling H-1B work visas.

International students generally need an H-1B work visa to stay in the U.S., which requires sponsorship from an employer. The program has become a target of the Trump administration, which is seeking to raise the fee for the visas to over $100,000.

Computer science graduate Collins Kibet, from Kenya, has sent out hundreds of applications and landed just a handful of interviews—mostly with AI bots. The Southern New Hampshire University graduate said that during the rare job interview with a person, the tone shifts when employers learn they would have to sponsor his H-1B work visa.

“Everybody just keeps quiet,” said Kibet, who started his own software company because he could not find a job.

Colleges are rethinking training for computer science students

Watching students navigate job searches has been hard for Nicholas Mattei, an associate computer science professor at Tulane. When he looks at some of the job ads, he thinks, “Really?”

“All the companies are coming back to us and saying, ‘Oh, well you need to train these people even better, and they need to be able to jump into a middle management role as opposed to an introductory or junior developer role,’” he said. “And it’s kind of crazy.”

Many colleges are retooling their computer science programs. With entry-level jobs going away, they are tasked with preparing students to do more.

To give students a leg up, professors at Georgia Tech researched what AT&T wanted and trained students for a month before they started internships with the company. The school plans to expand the effort for a program it will call “Bootcamp to Industry,” said Fisayo Omojokun, the associate dean for undergraduate education in the school’s College of Computing.

Staff tasked with recruiting businesses for College of Computing job fairs are also reaching out to a broader range of industries.

“Earlier this year, we got a call from a forestry company of all things,’” Omojokun said. “They’re like, ‘Hey, we are in forestry, and we know that AI can help in what we do in different ways.’”

title: Jimbōchō Book Town
description:
I visited Jimbōchō today, a neighborhood that’s home to more than 100 used bookstores. Many sell only Japanese books, but some of them have books in English or sell magazines, posters, or visual books that are interesting to browse no matter what language you speak. I visited maybe 20-30 of the stores; here are four of my favorites.

Sawaguchi Book Store features larger format books on art, design, photography, fashion, and architecture. The walls of the staircase are covered in wonderful posters; it took me awhile to climb those stairs. On the second floor, I found a Princess Mononoke movie poster for ¥50,000; tempting. Also on that floor, there’s a small seating area where you can enjoy a beverage out of their two vending machines and quietly read a book or look out the window.

Kitazawa Bookstore. A beautiful old bookstore selling mostly English titles. I spent a lot of time in here browsing. I found a nice leather-bound Pride and Prejudice and a copy of Hemingway’s For Whom the Bell Tolls from the 40s. They had these little notes scattered amongst the shelves gently reminding patrons of the store’s guidelines: “Here, silence helps words to grow. How eahc book with both hands, as if to embrace it.” Another one: “Don’t rush or force the pages wide. Stories, too, are most beautiful when they open slowly.”

Komiyama Shoten is another bookstore specializing in books about art, arcitecture, design, photography, and fashion. I found a cache of old Raygun magazines from the 90s along with a ton of other design books & magazines — on the third floor, I think. On that same floor, they have a collection of erotica and LGBTQ+ books, including a couple of amazing books by Tom of Finland. Lots of great posters throughout the store as well, including a poster for Kids (1995) signed by Larry Clark.

Ohya Shobu features books, woodblock prints, and maps from the Edo and Meiji periods. Super old stuff. The huge map of Edo (Tokyo) in the window is worth the trip by itself. Because everything was so ancient and presumably delicate, I was a bit timid about picking stuff up to look through it, but I’m gonna go back when I’m feeling bolder.

== Production ==
The original idea for ''Roy del espacio'' came from Ulises Pérez Aguirre, with Héctor López Carmona as director and cinematographer. Ernesto Cortázar was the films composer. Production of the film was from 1979 to 1982.<ref name="Brew">{{cite web|url=https://www.cartoonbrew.com/lost-films/roy-de-espacio-mexico-exclusive-clip-266629.html|title=Lost For 40 Years, Mexico’s Third Animated Feature, ‘Roy Del Espacio,’ Is Back With Help From Two Animators|last=Lang|first=Jamie|work=[[Cartoon Brew]]|date=16 September 2026|accessdate=23 September 2026}}</ref>

Multiples scenes of ''Roy del espacio'' were either of retraced scenes of older works or outright using footage without permission. These included the [[Flash Gordon (serial)|1936 ''Flash Gordon'' serial]] and the 1978 Japanese live-action [[space opera]] ''[[Message from Space]].<ref name="Brew"/>

title: Jev introduces a new shape of LLM—System One, aka Decision Models
description:
Simon Willison, Simon Willison's Weblog, Sept 23, 2026

Simon Willison discusses the latest AI fad, Jev, also known as "System One" models. "I'm with Maggie Appleton," he writes, "I think 'decision models' is a better name for these." Is basically black box AI. "Jev is an interesting variant on the usual LLM format: it still accepts text inputs, but instead of text output it returns floating point numbers corresponding to categories, yes/no questions, ratings, and associated confidence scores." As Willison notes, "It's great for anything that can be expressed as a classification task—think spam detection, suggesting labels, prioritization and ranking." Ah, that describes (sadly) so much educational activity (people have been going gaga over it in LinkedIn).

title: Trump administration attacks Australia's 'opt-out' algorithm law in rare intervention
description:
Cam Wilson, Sept 23, 2026

The U.S. government "wants US social media companies excluded from digital duty of care laws, which would give Australians the option to opt out of algorithmic feeds." Why would this matter? The algorithm is the difference between a social networking service that connects users with people and resources they want and a social networking service that is a channel for advertising and political messaging. Obviously there's a lot more money to be made by the latter, but it also causes a lot of harm. The public interest and social education are fulfilled much better by the former. At some point, instead of simply banning social media for children, people need to have the right to define and build their own algorithms, serving their own interests, without corporate and political interests intervening in the process.
